name: Chloe Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Chloe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the Riverside Homes office on Station Road by half eight, and the phones start before I've got my coat off. Riverside is a housing association, so it's tenants ringing about boilers, damp or a broken front door, and I book the repair and chase the contractor. Then it's filing tenancy forms, booking inspection visits for the housing officers, and typing up letters from the notes Denise (my manager) scribbles on yellow pads. I've been there two years and I'm still the slow one on the repairs system.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the tenants, even the shouty ones, because most of them just want someone to listen. What wears me out is the system freezing, the backlog, and knowing I'm on the lowest pay band in the building. Jonah, my partner, does nights at the supermarket depot, and between us we've got maybe two weeks of rent put by. There's also talk of merging our office with Eastgate, thirty miles away, and nobody will tell us straight what that means.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, maybe now they'll stop telling us a computer is about to sort everything out. I'd probably put a smug little message in the staff group chat. Our repair system can barely book a plumber as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means the same worries I've already got. The Eastgate merger was on the table before anyone said AI, and it's about money, not robots. If they close Station Road, I either drive an hour each way in a car I don't own, or I'm out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job the way I know it and not touch any new gadgets. I'd finally join the union this year and ask Marcus, our rep, whether the merger means redundancies. And Jonah and I would try to put 50 a month aside, though we've said that before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. Not scared of AI in that world, scared of the same old thing, which is one letter from head office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI would take over some routine tasks. Which bit of your day would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the repair booking, matching the job to a contractor and sending the tenant a text. That's a third of my day, if I'm honest. If that went I'd be left with the filing, and nobody keeps a person on for filing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tight, which bill goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone contract goes down to the cheapest one, then the Friday takeaway. Rent never goes unpaid. I type the arrears letters for tenants who fall behind, so I know exactly what happens if Jonah (her partner) and I miss a month.

say: I'd tell the group chat that AI was **mostly hype** after all.
I'd joke that our **repair system** can barely book a plumber, never mind think.
think: My real worry is the **Eastgate merger**, which is about money, not AI.
If Station Road closes, I'd face a **long commute** with no car, or **no job**.
Losing **repair booking** to software would leave me with a third less to do.
do: Join the **union** this year and ask the rep about merger redundancies.
Keep working the **old way** and avoid any new tools on the repairs system.
Try to save **50 a month** with Jonah, though they've failed before.
feel: She feels **tired** and braced for **bad news** from head office.
S0.quote: I type the arrears letters for tenants who fall behind, so I know exactly what happens if Jonah (her partner) and I miss a month.
fieldNote: Her anxiety predates AI: the **office merger** and **thin savings** drive it.
She knows her job from the inside: she writes the **arrears letters** she fears receiving.
Even a small AI change hits her, since **repair booking** is a third of her day.

steps.text: Join the housing staff union and ask Marcus about merger redundancies
Put 50 a month into a savings pot with Jonah
Keep booking repairs by phone the way she does now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when you let tech firms write the rules. At work I'd be the one saying tenants deserve a person on the phone, not a chatbot. Online I'd share whatever the union puts out about protecting jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm exactly the job they mean. Booking, checking, answering tenants, writing letters: that's my whole day in one list. Denise is kind, but if head office says one admin covers both offices with the new software, it won't be me, because I'm the slowest on the system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and push for a deal that nobody gets pushed out without retraining. I'd sign the petition, write to our councillor about housing staff, all of that. What I wouldn't do is sit at home learning chatbots, because I don't trust them and I'm bad at it. I'd start looking at the job ads, but there's nothing round here except the care home and the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's going soft. I'm angry, but under the anger I'm frightened, because I haven't got a plan B and I haven't got money for one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't learn the chatbots, but you're also the slowest on the system. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know, it doesn't add up. Part of me thinks if I refuse, they'll have to keep people like me. The other part knows they won't, and that I'm just being stubborn because I'm scared of looking stupid in front of Femi and the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about, apart from yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pauline on reception, who's 61 and still writes tenant numbers on her hand. And the tenants, honestly. Old Mr Okafor rings every Tuesday about his window, and a chatbot would just tell him his case is closed.

say: I'd say **tech firms** shouldn't get to write the rules on jobs.
I'd insist tenants deserve **a person** on the phone, not a **chatbot**.
think: My whole day is the list: **booking, checking, letters** and tenant calls.
If one admin covers **both offices**, it won't be me, as I'm **slowest**.
do: Attend every **union meeting** and push for **retraining** before any cuts.
Write to the **local councillor** about housing staff and sign the petition.
Scan **job ads**, though only the **care home** and depot are hiring nearby.
feel: She feels **angry** on top and **frightened** underneath, with no plan B.
S1.quote: Booking, checking, answering tenants, writing letters: that's my whole day in one list.
fieldNote: She recognises the card as a **description of her job**, task by task.
She admits her refusal to learn the tools is **fear of looking stupid**.
Her worry reaches **older colleagues** and **vulnerable tenants**, not just herself.

steps.text: Go to every union meeting and push for a no-cuts-without-retraining deal
Write to the local councillor about protecting housing office staff
Check job ads at the care home and the depot each week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness to let it happen with no plan, and that the government should have stopped it. I'd be posting about it constantly, and I'd be at any protest going. At work I'd ask head office straight out what happens to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be gone in the first wave, maybe within a year of it arriving. My job is all screen and phone, there's nothing hands-on in it at all, so the three years before the robots don't help me. Jonah's job at the depot is hands-on, so he'd last until about 2031, and then he'd go too. Two years' warning is no warning when you've got two weeks' rent saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's the truth. I'd probably try for the care home on Mill Lane, because wiping and lifting people is hands-on and the robots are three years behind. I'd ask my mum if we could move back in with her to save rent. And I'd be in the union and at the marches, because that's the only thing I know how to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like being on a bus with no brakes and everyone telling you to enjoy the view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try the care home. Have you thought about that work before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Never, and I'd be bad at it at first. My nan was in one, and the staff were run off their feet on rubbish pay. That's where everyone like me would go, so there'd be a queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonah that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we've got about three years where his wage carries both of us, and then nothing. Then I'd probably cry and he'd make toast, because that's what he does.

say: I'd say letting AGI arrive with **no plan** is madness and **government** should act.
I'd join **protests** and ask head office straight out what happens to staff.
think: My job is all **screen and phone**, so I'd be gone in the first wave.
Jonah's **depot job** lasts until robots arrive around **2031**.
**Two years** is no warning with **two weeks** of rent saved.
do: Apply to the **care home** on Mill Lane for hands-on work.
Ask her **mum** if she and Jonah can move in to save **rent**.
Stay active in the **union** and join every **march** going.
feel: She feels **sick** and out of control, with **no plan**.
S2.quote: My job is all screen and phone, there's nothing hands-on in it at all, so the three years before the robots don't help me.
fieldNote: She grasps the **thinking-first order** clearly: her job goes, Jonah's has **three years**.
She has **no plan** beyond care work, which she expects to be **crowded**.
Moving in with her **mum** is her only real safety net.

steps.text: Apply for care assistant shifts at the Mill Lane care home
Give notice on the Station Road flat and move in with her mum
Ask her mum to cover food while Jonah's wage covers bills
March with the union against job cuts at head office

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really, but louder and earlier. I'd say we've got five years to make the government put rules on this, so let's use them. I'd be at the union meetings saying exactly that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd probably still lose my job, just in 2030 instead of next year. The thinking AI comes for desk work first, so I'd be gone before Jonah. It gives us time to see it coming, but I'm not someone who's good with time. I tend to wait until things are on fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, the first year I'd do the union stuff and not much else. Maybe I'd do the free first-aid and care certificate at the college on Thursday nights, so I've got something for the care home. We'd try to save, but on our pay, saving means not eating out, and we already don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Less of a punch in the face than the two-year one, more like a weight I'd carry around every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wait until things are on fire. What would make you act sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If someone I knew got the push. If Pauline went, or one of the Eastgate lot, I'd panic. It's stupid, but I need to see AI take a real person's job, like Pauline (her colleague) on reception, before I'll sign up for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything those five years would let you and Jonah do that two wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe get Jonah his forklift and HGV licences, so he's on more money for the three years after my job goes. That's the only plan I can think of where we're not just waiting.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to force the government to set **rules**.
I'd repeat that message at every **union meeting** I attend.
think: I'd still lose my job, just around **2030** instead of next year.
Desk work goes before Jonah's hands-on job, so I'd be **first out**.
I tend to **wait until things burn**, so time doesn't help me much.
do: Take the **care certificate** course at the college on Thursday nights.
Help Jonah get **forklift and HGV** licences for better pay.
Keep up **union** work and push for rules on AI.
feel: It feels like a **heavy weight** carried every day, not a sudden blow.
S3.quote: I need to see AI take a real person's job, like Pauline (her colleague) on reception, before I'll sign up for anything.
fieldNote: She expects to lose her job even with **five years' warning**.
She admits she only acts once **someone she knows** is hit.
Her best plan rests on **Jonah's licences**, not her own career.

steps.text: Take the Thursday-night care certificate course at the town college
Push the union to campaign for national rules on AI at work
Wait to act on a new job until a colleague is cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse. Shorter working weeks, proper retraining paid for by the companies making the money. I'd say that at work and I'd share it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels like something that happens to a different version of me. I'd be 37. My office might not even exist by then because of the merger, never mind AI. So I'd worry, but it'd be a background worry, not a can't-sleep one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the care course at some point, maybe the second year. I'd keep doing my job the way I do it now, phone and paper. We'd want to save for a deposit, but honestly we'd be saving for rent, not a house. Jonah would get his licences.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in the back of my head. And a bit guilty, because I know I'd waste a lot of those ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 37 when it arrives and 40 when the robots come. What does your life look like then, in your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want kids by then, ideally. I'd probably be doing care work or something with my hands, because the office stuff will be gone first. Jonah would be at the depot until 2039, if he's lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your mind about learning the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if Riverside made it part of the job and paid us to learn. I won't learn the AI tools in my own time for free, because that's how bosses get you to train your own replacement.

say: I'd say **ten years** leaves no excuse for leaving workers behind.
I'd call for **shorter weeks** and retraining paid by the **AI companies**.
think: Ten years feels like it happens to a **different me**, aged **37**.
The **merger** might close my office before AGI even arrives.
I'd likely **waste** much of the decade, and I know it.
do: Take the **care course** in the second year of the decade.
Keep doing the job by **phone and paper** as now.
Learn AI tools only if Riverside **pays for training** in work hours.
feel: She feels a **background unease** and some **guilt** about wasting time.
S4.quote: I won't learn the AI tools in my own time for free, because that's how bosses get you to train your own replacement.
fieldNote: Ten years turns her fear into a **background worry**, but her job is still exposed.
Her refusal to learn tools is now framed as **not working for free**.
She hopes for **children** by 40 and expects hands-on work by then.

steps.text: Enrol on the care course at the college in year two
Keep handling repairs by phone and paper at Riverside
Ask the union to demand paid AI training in work hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years with two weeks' rent saved is a disaster. What would help is a guarantee that if your job goes, you get paid while you retrain, properly paid, not a leaflet. And somebody telling us the truth early, instead of Denise finding out from an email the same day we do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the money. If a computer does my job for nothing, somebody's saving my wage, and it isn't me or the tenants. Nobody ever asks the people at the bottom what we think, so thanks, I suppose.

headlineQuote: If a computer does my job for nothing, somebody's saving my wage, and it isn't me or the tenants.
portrait: Chloe is a **27-year-old** junior admin at a housing association office, earning the **lowest pay band**.
She and Jonah, a night-shift **depot worker**, have about **two weeks** of rent saved.
She distrusts AI tools and **never uses them**, partly from fear of looking slow.
She leans on the **union** and politics, and blames **tech firms** and bosses who keep savings.
Her mood runs from **anxious** in a plateau to **panicked** if AGI comes in two years.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, as two years' warning meets **two weeks** of rent saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** if her job goes, with a real wage, not a leaflet.
**Early, honest warning** from employers instead of same-day emails.
